fagopyrum-esculentum.summary: Buckwheat grows quickly into a soft, branching annual with arrowhead-shaped leaves and clusters of small white or pink-tinged flowers. Although its seeds are used like grain, it belongs to the knotweed family rather than the grasses. Farmers also grow it as a short-season cover crop, where its dense growth shades weeds and its flowers draw bees and other beneficial insects. Plants sometimes appear outside cultivation, especially on disturbed ground; that alone does not establish an invasive impact.

tandonia-budapestensis.summary: The Budapest slug is a slender, ground-dwelling slug often found around gardens, cultivated fields and other disturbed places. Its brownish-gray body is densely speckled, with a pale yellow ridge running down the tail. A dark stripe along the otherwise pale underside is especially useful when separating it from similar keeled slugs. It can feed both above and below the soil surface, damaging root crops, bulbs and newly sown seed. A curled, horseshoe-like resting posture is another helpful clue.

sources.label: John Innes Centre: Budapest keeled slug

nipaecoccus-nipae.summary: Buff coconut mealybugs look rather like tiny wax-covered cushions on their host plants. Adult females are orange to reddish brown, with yellowish wax and pointed tufts around the edge and across the back. Despite the common name, they feed on many plants, including palms, avocado and ornamental flowers. Their sap feeding produces sticky honeydew that can support black sooty mold, and ants may tend the colonies. Close inspection of a mature female is often needed to confirm the species.

cenchrus-ciliaris.summary: Buffelgrass forms coarse perennial clumps with rough leaves and fuzzy, bottlebrush-shaped seed heads. Originally planted as forage in dry regions, it is a serious problem in the Sonoran Desert, where it fills the spaces between native shrubs and cacti. Those connected patches carry fire through vegetation that is poorly adapted to burning. The seed heads change from reddish or purplish tones to tan as they mature, and seeds can travel on shoes, clothing, animals and moving water.

sources.label: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum: Save our saguaros

fallopia-baldschuanica.summary: Bukhara fleeceflower, also called silver lace vine, can cover a fence with a cloud of tiny pale flowers in late summer. This deciduous, twining climber has heart-shaped leaves and woody older stems. Its speed is part of its appeal in gardens, but also the reason it needs careful placement: shoots can scramble across nearby shrubs and quickly outgrow their support. Small winged fruits develop after flowering, often taking on a pink or reddish tint.

sources.label: University of Arkansas Extension: Silver lace vine

rhopalosiphoninus-latysiphon.summary: The bulb and potato aphid lives in places that are easy to overlook: around roots, inside stored bulbs and on potato tubers. It feeds on a wide range of plants, including ornamental bulbs such as tulips and gladiolus, and can affect crops both in the field and in storage. It is also associated with transmission of plant viruses. Because colonies may remain hidden below ground, careful inspection of planting material is more useful than looking only at the leaves.

sources.label: Petrovic-Obradovic and colleagues: First record in Serbia

watsonia-meriana.summary: Bulbil bugle-lily sends tall spikes of curved, trumpet-shaped flowers above fans of tough, swordlike leaves. This South African perennial grows from underground corms and is familiar in gardens for its salmon, pink, red or pale blooms. The bulbil-producing form develops small brown cormlets along the flower stems, each capable of starting another plant. In invaded open habitats, dense clumps can crowd out other vegetation; moving soil or dumping garden waste can carry the corms to new sites.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Watsonia meriana

poa-bulbosa.summary: Bulbous bluegrass is a small, cool-season grass that gets an early start in spring and dries out early as conditions warm. It grows in tufts, with narrow leaves ending in the little boat-shaped tips typical of bluegrasses. Many plants carry an unusual flowering head full of tiny leafy bulblets, rather than an ordinary-looking spray of seeds. These bulblets and the swollen bases of the shoots help it persist and spread. It occurs on disturbed ground and has also been used to stabilize eroding soil.

sources.label: University of Illinois Extension: Bulbous bluegrass

phalaris-aquatica.summary: Bulbous canarygrass, often called Harding grass, is a robust perennial that forms tall, leafy clumps topped by dense cylindrical flower heads. Slightly swollen shoot bases give it its other common name. Introduced from Mediterranean Europe as a forage grass, it has escaped into fields, ditches and streamside habitats. In affected western landscapes, established clumps compete with native vegetation for water and space. Most new plants arise from seed, although pieces of its short underground stems can also regrow.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Phalaris aquatica

cirsium-vulgare.summary: Bull thistle starts as a low rosette of prickly leaves, then raises a branching stem with pinkish-purple flower heads. Unlike creeping thistles, it has a taproot and spreads by seed. The leaves are rough and hairy above, woolly beneath, and tipped with sharp spines; spiny wings also run down the stems. Originally from Eurasia, it readily colonizes disturbed soil and heavily grazed ground. Its prickles discourage grazing and can make neighboring forage harder for animals to reach.

sources.label: University of Nevada Extension: Bull thistle
University of Florida: Thistle control in pastures

anthriscus-caucalis.summary: Bur chervil has delicate, fernlike leaves, but its small hooked fruits are its most useful calling card. This Eurasian herb commonly grows as an annual, with hollow, branching stems and little clusters of white flowers beside the upper leaves. The burrlike fruits catch on animals and help the plant travel beyond the parent patch. In parts of the western United States it can form dense growth along waterways and beneath shrubs, although it also survives in drier grassland.

sources.label: University of California: Bur and wild chervil
University of British Columbia E-Flora: Bur chervil

medicago-polymorpha.summary: Burclover spreads low across the ground, with three-parted leaves that can easily be mistaken for an ordinary clover. Small yellow flowers give way to tightly coiled pods, often armed with hooks that cling to fur and clothing. It grows in lawns, fields, roadsides and other disturbed places, and is also grown as forage or a cover crop. The same burrs that help disperse its seeds can become tangled in sheep's wool, reducing its value.

oplismenus-burmannii.summary: Burmann's basketgrass is a low annual grass with spreading stems and relatively broad leaves. The blades can look gently rippled across their width, a useful clue when the plant is not flowering. Its flower head is arranged as several short branches along a central stalk, with slender, often pinkish-red bristles extending well beyond the tiny spikelets. It can grow beside paths and in other disturbed places. Similar basketgrasses need careful comparison, especially when assessing a plant outside its familiar range.

sources.label: University of Richmond Kaxil Kiuic flora: Oplismenus burmannii

caryota-mitis.summary: Burmese fishtail palm gets its name from the jagged, fan-shaped leaflets that resemble little fish tails. Several slender trunks grow together in a clump, with new shoots arising at the base. Flowering follows an unusual sequence: a trunk flowers near its top first, then progressively lower down, and dies after its final flowering. The rest of the clump continues growing. Native to tropical Asia, this palm is widely cultivated in warm climates; its small fruits contain irritating material and should not be handled casually.

python-bivittatus.summary: Burmese pythons are large, muscular snakes patterned with dark, irregular patches on a tan background. They are comfortable in water and can be remarkably difficult to notice among wetland plants. Native to Southeast Asia, they have an established invasive population in southern Florida, where they eat a wide variety of mammals, birds and reptiles. Their broad diet is well documented: one study of digestive contents from more than 1,700 Florida pythons identified 76 prey species.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Burmese python
USGS: Diet of invasive Burmese pythons, 1995-2020

cayratia-japonica.summary: Bushkiller is a vigorous vine that uses tendrils to climb over shrubs, trees and garden structures. Its leaves have five toothed leaflets, and the small flowers are orange or salmon colored. The fleshy roots send up new shoots, particularly after they are disturbed, helping a patch recover even when the visible vines have been cut back. Native to Asia, Australia and nearby Pacific regions, it has escaped cultivation in the southern United States and is considered invasive in North Carolina.

eucalyptus-lehmannii.summary: Bushy yate is an evergreen eucalypt from Western Australia that grows as a bushy small tree or a many-stemmed mallee. Its smooth bark varies from pale pink and gray-brown to reddish tones, sometimes with older bark collected around the base. Cream, greenish or yellow flowers add a softer contrast to the foliage. In its native landscape it grows on exposed slopes, rocky outcrops, coastal dunes and creek beds; it is also planted as an ornamental tree elsewhere.

sources.label: Botanic Gardens of South Australia: Bushy yate

linaria-vulgaris.summary: Butter and eggs is the familiar yellow toadflax, with pale yellow, snapdragon-shaped flowers and a deeper orange-yellow center. Slender leaves line its upright stems, and each flower carries a long spur at the back. Once grown as an ornamental and dye plant, it now occurs along roadsides, in fields and in other open ground across much of temperate North America. A spreading root system lets it form persistent patches, making a few flowering stems part of a much larger plant.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Butter and eggs

bauhinia-purpurea.summary: Butterfly tree is also known as purple orchid-tree, and both names fit: its rounded leaves are split into two lobes, while its showy flowers range from pink to deep purple. This small to medium tree comes from India and Myanmar and is widely planted in warm regions. Long, flat seedpods follow the flowers and may remain on the branches through winter. In Florida it has escaped cultivation and is considered invasive, so its ornamental appeal needs to be weighed against local spread.

ophiognomonia-clavigignenti-juglandacear.summary: Butternut canker fungus attacks the bark of butternut trees, creating dead, sunken areas that can gradually encircle branches and trunks. Early damage may appear around leaf scars or wounds; older cankers become long cracks or open, dark-stained patches edged with ridges of living bark. As the disease advances, branches die back and the crown thins. Spores move between trees in rain splash and by other carriers. The disease has caused severe losses of butternut across its eastern North American range.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Butternut branch dieback

soliva-anthemifolia.summary: Button burrweed stays close to the ground, forming small patches of finely divided, fernlike leaves. Its flowers are easy to miss because the heads sit together near the plant's center rather than rising on showy stalks. As the fruits mature, the clusters become buttonlike and woolly, with stiff pointed tips. This South American annual has become established in disturbed ground and pastures elsewhere. Mature fruit is especially useful for separating it from other small burrweeds with a similar leafy appearance.

sources.label: New South Wales Flora Online: Soliva anthemifolia
Flora of New Zealand: Soliva anthemifolia

impatiens-walleriana.summary: Busy lizzy is a soft-stemmed tropical perennial best known as a colorful bedding plant for shady gardens. Compact mounds of glossy foliage carry flowers in white, pink, red, orange and many cultivated combinations, often from late spring until frost. In colder climates it is usually grown as an annual. Ripe capsules release their seeds suddenly, giving the genus its 'impatient' name. Common garden impatiens can suffer from downy mildew, which yellows the leaves and may leave plants nearly bare.

brassica-oleracea.summary: Cabbage belongs to a remarkably varied species that also includes kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi. Centuries of cultivation have emphasized different parts of the same basic plant: leaves, flower buds or swollen stems. The leaves are usually thick and waxy, often blue-green, and flowering plants carry yellow, four-petaled blossoms followed by long pods. Wild cabbage and garden forms may look quite different, so a tight leafy head is only one possible expression of this species.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin: Growing cole crops

hellula-undalis.summary: Cabbage webworm is a small moth whose caterpillars feed on cabbage and other mustard-family plants. The larvae are pale gray-yellow with several darker stripes running lengthwise, and they shelter in silk among the young leaves. Feeding near the growing point is particularly damaging: young plants may be stunted or develop several small heads instead of one normal head. The adults are brownish moths with pale wing markings, but closely related webworms can look very similar.

sources.label: University of Hawaii Crop Knowledge Master: Hellula undalis
University of Georgia IPM: Cabbage webworm

pieris-rapae.summary: The small white butterflies visiting a vegetable patch may be the parents of imported cabbageworms. Their velvety green caterpillars blend into cabbage, broccoli, and related crops, often resting along a leaf vein before chewing holes between the veins. Older larvae do most of the damage and can work their way into developing heads. A regular look beneath the leaves can catch them early; handpicking caterpillars and using well-fitted row covers are useful options for a home garden.

psylliodes-chrysocephalus.summary: Cabbage-stem flea beetles feed on wild and cultivated members of the mustard family. Adults chew the leaves, while their larvae tunnel inside leaf stalks and stems, so the same pest can cause damage in two quite different places. The beetles are usually shiny metallic blue with orange-red legs, although pale and mixed-color forms occur. They are especially important in oilseed rape, where heavy feeding on newly emerged seedlings can destroy the growing point before plants have a chance to recover.

sources.label: AHDB: Cabbage stem flea beetle in oilseed rape

cactoblastis-cactorum.summary: Cactus moth caterpillars live together inside prickly pear pads, hollowing them out as they feed. Older larvae are bright orange-red with dark bands, a striking contrast to the unobtrusive gray-brown adult moth. Females stack eggs into slender sticks that can resemble cactus spines. Introduced from South America to control unwanted cacti in some countries, the moth became a threat where native prickly pears are important parts of the landscape. Infested pads may yellow, ooze fluid and shed piles of insect droppings.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: South American cactus moth

tenebroides-mauritanicus.summary: Cadelle beetles live among stored grain and other dry foods, where both the insects and the places they hide deserve attention. The shiny dark adults have a noticeable narrow waist behind the front part of the body; the pale larvae have a black head and dark markings. Feeding damages grain kernels, especially the germ. Larvae can also bore into nearby wood or plaster, creating sheltered places that make an infestation harder to clear. Old grain residues and damaged storage surfaces are useful places to inspect.

urena-lobata.summary: Caesarweed has small pink flowers that look like miniature hibiscus blooms, but its hooked fruits are often the more memorable feature. They cling to clothing and animal fur, carrying seeds away from the parent shrub. Rough, sometimes lobed leaves and hairy stems help distinguish it before fruit forms. This widespread tropical plant grows in disturbed places, pastures, and forest openings; Florida treats it as invasive. Brush seeds from clothing and equipment before leaving a patch, and keep seed-bearing cuttings contained during removal.

acorus-calamus.summary: Sweet flag grows at wetland edges in clumps of upright, sword-shaped leaves. A short, fleshy spike of tiny flowers appears to project from the side of a leaflike stalk, an unusual feature worth photographing. Names matter here: introduced Acorus calamus has often been confused in North American records with the native American sweet flag, Acorus americanus. The introduced form described by the sources spreads through rhizomes and is sterile. Have a wetland plant specialist confirm the identification before removing a stand or moving divisions.

eulecanium-cerasorum.summary: Calico scale earns its name from the white patches on a dark, rounded adult female. These sap-feeding insects settle on deciduous trees, and their sticky honeydew can leave leaves and objects beneath the tree coated with black sooty mold. Young scales spend part of the season on leaves, then move onto twigs to overwinter. A few scales may do little harm, so check the tree's condition as well as the insects. If treatment is needed, monitoring for tiny moving crawlers helps identify the useful window.

ligustrum-ovalifolium.summary: Oval-leaved privet is a dense hedge shrub with glossy leaves, fragrant white flower clusters, and small fruits that ripen dark purple-black. Its foliage usually remains through mild winters, giving an escaped plant the same tidy-looking greenery as a garden hedge. The species comes from eastern Asia and is recorded outside cultivation in regional floras. Young shoots are nearly hairless, a useful clue alongside the broad oval leaves. Where seedlings appear beyond a planting, remove them early and prune unwanted flowers before fruit develops.

aonidiella-aurantii.summary: California red scale can look like a scattering of tiny reddish-brown disks on citrus leaves, twigs, or fruit. Each disk shelters a sap-feeding insect; newly hatched crawlers move before settling and building their own protective cover. Heavy infestations weaken plants and blemish fruit, but parasitoid wasps often provide valuable control. Look closely before treating a tree, because scale covers can remain after the insect dies. A local crop adviser can help check whether scales are alive and time any treatment to the vulnerable crawler stage.

zantedeschia-aethiopica.summary: The white 'flower' of a calla lily is a curved leaflike spathe wrapped around a yellow spike of many tiny flowers. Large arrow-shaped leaves rise from thick underground rhizomes, forming lush clumps in moist ground. This southern African plant is widely grown for gardens and cut flowers. Its ability to grow from rhizomes matters when a planting is removed: leftover pieces should not be dumped beside streams or wetlands. Wear gloves when handling it, and keep the irritating plant material away from children and pets.

pyrus-calleryana.summary: Callery pear is conspicuous in spring when clusters of white flowers cover the branches before or around leaf-out. Glossy, rounded leaves follow, along with small hard fruits that birds can carry beyond planted trees. Familiar cultivars such as Bradford belong to this species, and crossing between compatible trees has helped escaped populations spread. Wild seedlings may develop formidable thorns and form dense growth in fields and disturbed places. Replacing a planted tree with a locally appropriate alternative helps reduce seed sources; removal also needs a plan for sprouts.

sources.label: Callery pear: history, identification and control

lepidosaphes-camelliae.summary: Camellia scale hides beneath small brown, oystershell-shaped covers on the undersides of leaves. Camellias, sasanquas, and hollies are among its hosts, and heavy infestations can make foliage drop. Tiny crawlers briefly move about before settling to feed, while older insects remain protected under their covers. It is easy to confuse this species with other armored scales, so a close photograph or sample is useful. Inspect incoming plants and preserve the lady beetles and parasitic wasps that help keep scale populations down.

sources.label: Lepidosaphes tapleyi: comparison with L. camelliae

alhagi-maurorum.summary: Camelthorn is a thorny perennial with an underground reach far greater than its modest height suggests. Its stiff branches carry small gray-green leaves and pink to maroon pea flowers; the pods narrow between the seeds like a string of beads. Deep roots and spreading underground stems help it persist in dry ground and colonize irrigated fields or ditch banks. Cutting the top is rarely the end of the job. Keep soil and root fragments from moving to clean areas and plan follow-up with a local weed specialist.

aspidiotus-duplex.summary: Camphor scale is an armored scale that can hide in plain sight as small brown bumps on ornamental plants. The female's rounded, raised cover usually has a yellow-orange spot toward one side, while the male's cover is more elongated. Despite the common name, its hosts include camellias, citrus, and many other plants as well as camphor trees. Older references call it Aspidiotus duplex; modern accounts use Pseudaonidia duplex. Inspect new plants carefully, and have a sample identified before choosing a scale treatment.

cnestus-mutilatus.summary: Sometimes called the gas-can beetle, this small ambrosia beetle is drawn to ethanol odors, including those released by stressed trees. Females bore into wood and cultivate fungi that feed their young. The reddish-brown adults are only a few millimeters long, so fresh entry holes and boring dust may attract attention first. Its unusual habit of also boring into some plastic fuel containers explains the nickname. In a landscape, investigate the condition of affected trees and obtain an identification before assuming every tiny hole has the same cause.

cinnamomum-camphora.summary: Camphor tree is a broad evergreen with glossy leaves that release a distinctive camphor scent when crushed. Three strong veins often stand out near the leaf base, and small dark fruits attract birds that carry the seeds. Originally from Asia, it can become a large shade tree; in Florida, escaped trees invade disturbed ground and forests. Small seedlings are easier to address than mature trees, which can resprout after cutting. Where it is invasive, choose another shade tree and check nearby woodland for young plants.

poa-compressa.summary: Canada bluegrass is a low, spreading perennial whose flattened stems give it another helpful name: flat-stemmed bluegrass. It forms loose turf through underground rhizomes and carries compact, branched seed heads above narrow leaves. Poor, disturbed ground often suits it better than the richer soils favored by some other pasture grasses. Despite its common name, the botanical account treats it as introduced in North America. For an unfamiliar patch, photograph the stem, leaf junction and seed head before deciding how it fits a lawn or restoration site.

cirsium-arvense.summary: Canada thistle builds patches from a spreading root system, so the shoots above ground show only part of the plant. Spiny leaves and clusters of small purple flower heads help identify it, but its persistent underground buds explain why a single mowing or digging rarely succeeds. It competes in crops, pastures, and disturbed ground, and livestock often avoid grazing around prickly patches. Prevent seed production, keep root-contaminated soil from moving, and combine repeated follow-up with healthy competing vegetation to gradually weaken an established stand.

phoenix-canariensis.summary: Canary Island date palm makes a striking silhouette: a stout trunk topped by a broad crown of long, arching feather leaves. Mature trunks show diamond-shaped scars from old leaf bases, while female trees bear clusters of small yellow-orange dates. Native to the Canary Islands, it is widely planted in warm climates and can naturalize where conditions suit it. The sharp spines at the base of each leaf deserve respect. Leave work high in the crown to a qualified arborist and watch for seedlings beyond the intended planting.

hypericum-canariense.summary: Canary Island St. John's wort is a woody shrub with narrow leaves and clusters of bright yellow flowers. Unlike the low-growing St. John's worts many gardeners know, it can reach several meters tall. In coastal California, escaped plantings form dense stands in disturbed grassland and scrub, crowding native vegetation. Both underground spread and abundant seed complicate removal. Photograph the flowers, leaves and stem shape before acting, then work with local land managers to prevent seed production and revisit treated patches for new growth.

delphinium-elatum.summary: Tall delphinium brings upright spires of blue to purplish flowers above a clump of deeply divided leaves. This perennial comes from Europe and Asia and is the source of many garden selections, so cultivated plants can vary markedly in height and flower color. Its tall stems appreciate shelter and support, especially in wind or heavy rain. Remove spent spikes if you do not want seed, and keep all parts away from grazing animals or curious pets: this beautiful member of the buttercup family is toxic if eaten.

aleurites-moluccanus.summary: Candlenut, or kukui, is a broad-crowned tropical tree whose pale green foliage can stand out across a wooded valley. Younger leaves are often lobed, while older leaves may be more oval. Small pale flowers give way to rounded fruits enclosing hard, dark seeds rich in oil—the source of the name candlenut. Long valued in Pacific cultures, it is naturalized in Hawaii and holds special cultural significance there. Fallen seeds readily produce seedlings, so watch planting boundaries and avoid distributing unwanted fruit or soil containing seeds.

rhinella-marina.summary: Cane toads are large, warty amphibians that often appear around gardens, buildings, and water after dark. Their broad glands behind the eyes can release a milky toxin when threatened, making an encounter dangerous for a pet that bites one. Introduced populations are a management concern in Florida and other warm regions. Smaller native toads can look similar, so size alone is not enough for identification. Keep pet food indoors, supervise pets outside, and photograph an unfamiliar toad before seeking local wildlife guidance.

rhabdoscelus-obscurus.summary: The New Guinea sugarcane weevil spends its most damaging stage hidden inside a plant. Pale, legless larvae tunnel through sugarcane and palms, often leaving a plug of fibers at a tunnel entrance. Feeding can weaken palm trunks or damage the growing tip, so the first visible sign may be a declining or unstable plant. The species has moved among tropical islands, with transported palms providing a pathway. Keep suspect plants on site and ask an agricultural or plant-health specialist to identify the insect before moving or treating them.

pouteria-campechiana.summary: Canistel is a tropical fruit tree best known for its golden-yellow fruit and rich, sometimes egg-yolk-like flesh. The glossy leaves are simple and smooth-edged, and small cream flowers sit in their axils. Fruits vary from rounded to spindle-shaped, often ending in a point; several glossy brown seeds lie inside. Garden trees benefit from room to grow and good drainage. Pick fruit at the appropriate mature stage and let it soften before eating, and keep an eye on self-sown seedlings around a planting.

sources.label: Canistel growing in the Florida home landscape

cucumis-melo.summary: Cantaloupes, honeydews, and several less familiar melons all belong to Cucumis melo, a warm-season vine with tendrils, rough leaves, and small yellow flowers. Fruit shape, rind and flesh vary greatly among cultivated groups, so a netted orange-fleshed melon is only one version of the species. Bees and other insects help flowers set fruit. In a garden, give the vines sun, space and well-drained soil, and avoid excess nitrogen that produces lush growth at the expense of fruit.

sources.label: Flower and fruit set in cucurbits
